Skop emphasized that Georgia's abortion laws, as well as those of every other state, are very clear that an abortion can be done to save the life of the mother. Further, she said the laws do not apply to abortion procedures such as dilation and curettage if the unborn baby is already dead, as was the case for Thurman.

"The law states again that a miscarriage is an exception. It also states that an ectopic pregnancy is an exception. So we should never be reading of women not getting miscarriage care or not getting ectopic pregnancies treated because they are clearly an exception in every pro-life state's laws," Skop said.

Skop said that it's the distortions of the laws that have done harm to women, not the laws themselves, leaving women like Miller unsure about seeking life-saving care and doctors unsure about giving it.

"The lies about pro-life laws are hurting women. The pro-life laws are not hurting women, but the lies are hurting women. Because in many cases, the women do not understand. And we've seen that sometimes even the doctors don't understand. They're not reading the law. They're listening to the pro-abortion media," Skop said.

Dr. Christina Francis, CEO of the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists, made similar comments on Fox & Friends Saturday.

"We are seeing the direct results of spreading lies and misinformation about these laws. Women are being harmed by that because they are delaying in seeking care. And so I think it's really important, no matter where somebody stands on the issue of abortion, we should all want women to have accurate information so that they seek care immediately if they're experiencing complications from things like these high-risk abortion drugs," Francis said.

ProPublica defended their story in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying, "We stand by our reporting. The state's committee of more than 30 experts concluded that the deaths of Amber Thurman and Candi Miller were preventable, a newsworthy finding. Our ongoing reporting is illuminating the challenges doctors face in caring for patients with pregnancy complications in states with restricted access to abortion."

In April, President Donald Trump followed through on a campaign promise and implemented tariffs on the majority of the United States' trading partners. Predictably, the left lost their collective minds and giddily spoke of the coming collapse of the American economy, higher inflation and massive unemployment.

Perhaps no one on the left stoked fear more than the Democrat senator from Hawaii, Brian Schatz. Schatz lamented that, "Donald Trump is ruining the economy on purpose … we'll be paying more for everything — groceries, food, cars, homes, toys, electronics, everything that you buy. This is about the ability for people to pay for college. This is about the ability for people to retire with dignity and comfort. Trillions of dollars of wealth are being demolished."

Schatz may be a liberal senator from the Rainbow state, but he is apparently no Nostradamus. The American economy is doing quite well and shows no signs of slowing down.

The United States added nearly 140,000 new jobs in May 2025, beating forecasts and the unemployment rate remained at 4.2%. Since February 2025, the first full month of Trump's second term, the United States has added more than 515,000 jobs, despite shrinking the size of the Federal Government.

Inflation remains low as well. The Consumer Price Index, a measure of inflation, was 2.4% for the 12 months ending in May 2025, slightly up from the 2.3% number in April. Core inflation was at 2.8% for the third straight months, growing at the slowest pace since inflation surged in the spring of 2021.

Inflation was held down by declines in airfare, new and used cars, clothing and energy costs.

The positive job news and low inflation have caused consumer confidence to surge. Consumer confidence rose 12.3 points in May to a reading of 98, the Conference Board said in its latest survey, the first monthly gain since November and the biggest monthly increase since March 2021. The reading of 98 was significantly higher than economists' prediction of 88.

U.S. small-business confidence improved in May. The National Federation of Independent Business said that its Small Business Optimism Index increased three points to 98.8 last month, rising for the first time since December 2024.

After reaching a historic peak in the last quarter of 2024, credit card balances are improving across the nation. Credit card balances fell to $1.18 trillion in the first quarter of 2025, down $29 billion, or 2.4% from the previous quarter. Gas prices are currently below $3 in 29 states.

So no, Senator Schatz, Trump has not destroyed the economy. The economy is adding jobs. Inflation is lower under Trump than under former President Joe Biden. Consumer and small business confidence is increasing, and Americans are even starting to pay down their credit card debt.

Given the June 11 announcement of a trade deal between the United States and China, we should expect to see confidence improve, continued investment in the country by businesses, and more jobs to be created. The United States' economy is robust and resilient.

A new report from the Council of Economic Advisers found that the prices of imported goods have fallen this year and have dipped faster than overall goods prices since February.

The CEA, an agency within the Executive Office of the President, said its findings contradict claims that the Trump administration's tariffs on many countries around the world or fears sparked by the levies would lead to a rise in inflation.

The report breaks down the Personal Consumption Expenditure Price Index, which is an inflation gauge watched closely by the Federal Reserve and financial markets, and the Consumer Price Index, into imported and domestic components.

Overall goods prices in the PCE index jumped by 0.4% from December through May, which corresponds to a 1% annualized rate. Meanwhile, the imported component of PCE goods prices dropped by 0.1% during that same time period.

The report said similar analysis for the CPI showed that imported goods dipped 0.8% while overall goods prices remained flat.

The CEA report said it compared the imported subindex to overall prices from December through May to capture the effects of President Donald Trump's policies in his second administration.

"The results clearly show the price of imported components declining, starting in March, while overall prices were close to unchanged or increased slightly," the report reads. "Cumulatively, overall PCE prices have increased by about 1.1% since December compared to about 0.2% for PCE import prices."

The CEA also acknowledged that its analysis "does not identify the counterfactual in which tariffs are not instituted."

"Goods and imported goods prices started to diverge towards the end of 2023, and have continued since," the report says. "Importantly, there is no clear trend break so far this year. This analysis suggests that tariffs have not reduced the disinflationary impulse from imported goods as of May."

A year ago today, President Donald Trump announced a sweeping new round of global tariffs, escalating trade tensions with key allies and adversaries alike, raising fresh concerns about the outlook for the U.S. and global economy.

The "Liberation Day" tariffs were introduced as a broad set of import taxes that Trump said would correct long-standing trade imbalances and reduce U.S. reliance on foreign goods.

In the months that followed, markets experienced bouts of volatility as businesses and investors adjusted to the shifting trade landscape. Policymakers and economists, meanwhile, debated the longer-term impact on growth, inflation and global trade flows.

Many economists warned of potential consequences, including higher prices, slower growth and rising uncertainty for businesses and investors.

But not everyone agreed. "Trump proved 12 Nobel Prize economists wrong," economist Stephen Moore told Fox News Digital. "Inflation didn't rise. Why? Because the tax cuts, deregulation and 'drill, baby, drill' policies lowered prices and offset the tariffs," added Moore, a former Trump adviser and co-founder of Unleash Prosperity.

Former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers called the tariffs "masochistic," saying they were the worst levy the U.S. had imposed in decades. "Never before has an hour of Presidential rhetoric cost so many people so much," Summers wrote on X.

Paul Krugman, a Nobel Prize-winning economist, said Trump had "gone full-on crazy" in the hours after the "Liberation Day" tariffs were announced. "If you had any hopes that Trump would step back from the brink, this announcement, between the very high tariff rates and the complete falsehoods about what other countries do, should kill them."

Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, warned that the tariffs would be "negative the world over." She said Trump's trade policy would weigh on global growth. "It will not be good for the global economy, and it will not be good for those who impose the tariffs or those who retaliate," Lagarde said.

Joseph Stiglitz said Trump's tariff threats have made the U.S. "a scary place to invest" and could unleash stagflation. "I cannot see a really robust economy," said Stiglitz. "I see the global economy suffering greatly from the uncertainty that Trump poses."

Allianz chief economic adviser Mohamed El-Erian called for clarity from the White House. "If we get clarity on this, this is an economy that can adjust," he told FOX Business.

Bill Gross, the co-founder of PIMCO, said the latest round of tariffs is "similar to going off the gold standard in 1971" — an "epic" shift that markets won't quickly recover from. "It's not something where you can time a market bottom quickly," Gross told CNBC.

Iran says it is closing the Strait of Hormuz again to commercial vessels and that any ship that approaches it will be targeted.

The closure came as reports emerged of vessels in or near the strait being targeted by Tehran. The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps blamed a continuing US blockade for its decision, which comes a day after Iran's foreign minister announced the key global shipping channel had been temporarily reopened.

US President Donald Trump said Iran cannot "blackmail" the US with threats regarding the waterway, which Tehran has effectively blocked for nearly two months — causing global energy prices to soar.

The IRGC Navy warned that "no vessel is to move from its anchorage in the Persian Gulf or the Sea of Oman." It said a number of vessels had passed through the strait since Friday night, but that it would shut again until the US stopped its blockade of Iranian ports. "Approaching the Strait of Hormuz will be considered co-operation with the enemy, and the offending vessel will be targeted," the IRGC added.

Trump said on Friday that a naval blockade of Iranian ports would continue until a peace deal was agreed. The US said it had turned away 23 ships since it began enforcing the blockade on 13 April.

Iran's Supreme National Security Council said this was a violation of the ceasefire agreement and that it would stop the reopening of the strait while it was still in place.

There have been several reports of vessels being attacked. Two Iranian gunboats opened fire on a tanker in the strait. A container ship was also hit by "an unknown projectile" off the north-eastern coast of Oman. India's foreign ministry said it had summoned the Iranian ambassador to convey its "deep concern at the shooting incident today involving two Indian-flagged ships."

About 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas is usually transported through the strait, but the number of ships making the journey has dramatically decreased during the recent conflict. The narrow chokepoint connects the Gulf to the Arabian Sea and is the only way to reach several oil-producing states by sea. The crisis has seen the price of a barrel of oil surge above $100 at points.

US President Donald Trump has signed his landmark policy bill into law, a day after it was narrowly passed by Congress.

The signing event at the White House on Friday afternoon enacts key parts of the Trump agenda including tax cuts, spending boosts for defence and the immigration crackdown.

There was a celebratory atmosphere at the White House as Trump signed the bill ahead of Independence Day fireworks and a military picnic attended by the pilots who recently flew into Iran to strike three nuclear sites.

Trump told supporters it will unleash economic growth, but he must now convince sceptical Americans as polling suggests many disapprove of parts of the bill.

Several members of his own Republican party were opposed because of the impact on rising US debt and Democrats warned the bill would reward the wealthy and punish the poor.

The 870-page package includes: extending 2017 tax cuts from Trump's first term; steep cuts to Medicaid spending, the state-provided healthcare scheme for those on low incomes and the disabled; new tax breaks on tipped income, overtime and Social Security; a budget increase of $150bn for defence; a reduction in Biden-era clean energy tax credits; and $100bn to Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In a speech from the White House balcony, Trump thanked Republican lawmakers who helped usher the bill to his desk. He touted the tax cuts in the bill, brushing aside criticism of the impact to social programmes such as food assistance and Medicaid. "The largest spending cut, and yet, you won't even notice it," he said of the bill. "The people are happy."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries delayed the final vote by speaking for nearly nine hours. He called the bill an "extraordinary assault on the healthcare of the American people."

Only two Republicans went against, joining all 212 Democrats united in opposition. The bill passed by 218 votes to 214. Earlier, the Senate passed the bill but US Vice-President JD Vance was required to cast a tiebreaking vote after three Republicans held out.

"There could be no better birthday present for America than the phenomenal victory we achieved just hours ago," Trump told supporters in Des Moines.

Analysis by the Congressional Budget Office suggests the tax cuts could produce a surplus in the first year but will then cause the deficit to rise sharply. According to the Tax Policy Center, about 60% of the benefits would go to those making above $217,000. Changes to Medicaid would result in nearly 12 million losing coverage in the next decade, the CBO estimates.

Polling taken before the bill passed suggests public support is low. A recent Quinnipiac University survey pointed to only 29% endorsing the legislation.

On a bright Tehran spring day, Sanaei Ghaznavi street, with its mix of shops selling groceries and household goods alongside fast food and flowers, seems like an everyday place. In a country where lives have long been buffeted by crises, it is a snapshot of a people just trying to get through the day while their future hangs on forces beyond their control.

For Mohammad, in t-shirt and jeans, even cranking open the striped awning of his family's shoe shop is an act of hope. "It makes me happy to be in here," he tells us. "So many people have lost their jobs and aren't working." And there are few customers. "We had so many before," his father Mustafa laments as he explains this business has been in their family for 40 years.

One Iranian website recently cited an unofficial estimate that up to four million jobs may have been lost or impacted by the combined effect of the war and the government's near-total internet shutdown.

"People are paying three times more for a loaf of bread now," moans Shahla, an elderly woman. "People are going through hell now just to pay for bread." She casts her eyes across the leafy street. "People who are well off, they're okay, but not for workers who don't earn much."

I ask what her message to the negotiators is. "Stop it, that's enough," she declares. "I don't think something good will come of it for us because Trump is just threatening people."

Security has visibly tightened. Plain-clothed security from the paramilitary volunteer Basij, or the Islamic Revolutionary Guards, are ubiquitous now.

Small demonstrations against the rising cost of living in late 2025 built into a nationwide outbreak of anti-government protest earlier this year, with several thousand people killed in the resulting security crackdown.

"It was scary during the war," recounts Ali. "We felt alone. Our families were in other Iranian cities and we couldn't reach them." His sister tells us she just quit her job as a chef because the restaurant owner said he could no longer pay her.

"I love President Trump and I hate President Trump," Ali announces. "I love him because he said he would help the people of Iran. I hate him because he didn't."

At a square nearby, one woman rises and declares: "We only negotiate with President Trump from our position of strength." Mustafa the shoe salesman sums it up simply: "We just want this war to end."

Lebanon's prime minister has accused Israel of war crimes after Israeli air strikes killed one journalist and wounded another in southern Lebanon on Wednesday.

The strike killed Amal Khalil, who worked for Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar, and injured freelance photographer Zeinab Faraj. Officials in Lebanon say they were deliberately targeted as they sought shelter in a home after an initial air strike hit the vehicle in front of them, killing two men.

The officials also accused the Israel Defense Forces of intentionally targeting a marked ambulance as it tried to reach the journalists.

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said: "Targeting journalists, obstructing access to them by relief teams, and even targeting their locations again after these teams arrive constitutes described war crimes." He accused Israel of repeatedly targeting media workers in southern Lebanon in what he described as "an established approach."

In a statement, the IDF said it "does not target journalists and acts to mitigate harm to them while maintaining the safety and security of its troops." The IDF said it identified two vehicles that had "departed from a military structure used by Hezbollah."

Clayton Weimer, the executive director of Reporters Without Borders, said: "The Red Cross signalled they were unable to get through because of ongoing Israeli bombardment. So that is callous disregard, on top of what appears to be a deliberate and targeted killing of a journalist."

The US-based Committee to Protect Journalists said it was "outraged" by Khalil's death. "The repeated strikes on the same location, the targeting of an area where journalists were sheltering, and the obstruction of medical and humanitarian access constitute a grave breach of international humanitarian law."

At least 2,475 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Lebanon since the latest war began. Israeli authorities say Hezbollah attacks have killed two civilians in Israel since 2 March, and that 13 Israeli soldiers have been killed in combat in Lebanon. Israeli attacks have killed seven journalists in Lebanon, according to the CPJ.

Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines, will stand trial for crimes against humanity after judges at the International Criminal Court confirmed his charges.

The 81-year-old is accused of the extrajudicial killing of thousands during his deadly "war on drugs" between 2011 and 2019. Those charges were "unanimously confirmed" by pre-trial judges, who had "substantial grounds to believe" that Duterte had committed the alleged crimes.

The confirmation comes after several appeals by the ex-president to be released from detention, where he has been held for more than a year. Duterte has refused to recognise the ICC proceedings, arguing that during his presidency in 2019 the Philippines had pulled out of the Rome Statute, the ICC's founding agreement.

But judges ruled that the court could still hear Duterte's case, given that the alleged crimes had happened between 2011 and 2019 — while the Philippines was still a member of the ICC. Judges also authorised more than 500 victims to take part in proceedings.

At the heart of the trial is Duterte's "war on drugs" campaign, which human rights groups say targeted and killed small-time drug dealers while failing to nab the kingpins. Duterte has denied the allegations, condemning the charges as "an outrageous lie." The police maintained that they only killed in self-defence.

Duterte's lawyers had argued that the former president was unfit to participate in ICC proceedings due to cognitive impairment. But ICC judges rejected the argument and said they believed Duterte was fit to take part.

Leila de Lima, a member of the Philippines' House of Representatives and one of Duterte's staunchest critics, said the confirmation marked "a great day for the fighters against impunity and state-sponsored violence."

"The wheels of justice should have not taken this long to turn. But we take what we are dealt with for the sake of the rule of law," she said. Human rights organisation KARAPATAN described it as "vindication of the Filipino people's efforts to uphold and pursue justice and accountability."

A total of 518 people died in Tanzania from "unnatural causes" in the wake of widespread protests that followed last year's general elections, the commission of inquiry set up to investigate the violence has announced.

However, commission chairman Mohamed Chande Othman did not say who was responsible for the deaths and recommended further investigations.

Opposition parties and human rights groups have accused the security forces of unleashing a brutal crackdown on anti-government protesters.

President Samia Suluhu Hassan was declared the winner of the 29 October election with 98% of the vote — which the opposition described as a "mockery" of democracy. The president said the election was fair and transparent. She blamed foreigners for the violence and said it was part of a plot to overthrow her.

Most of those who died — 490 — were male, Othman said. The commission identified several causes of the violence, citing economic, political and social issues, including demands for political reforms, unemployment and "lack of patriotism."

It said politicians and activists used these issues to persuade citizens to take part in protests. It added that the protests were neither peaceful nor lawful and would not qualify for legal protection.

Othman said the violence was the result of multiple factors, some of which have existed for many years. "We are dealing with both long-standing issues that have persisted over time and immediate triggers that ignited tensions on the ground," he said.

Opposition parties have raised concerns about the nine-member commission, appointed by President Samia, accusing it of lacking independence and impartiality to investigate the violence. The commission collected evidence from across the country from ordinary citizens, victims, political leaders and security agencies.

Coventry chairman Doug King says Sky Blues fans should not worry about "what may or may not happen" after head coach Frank Lampard was linked with a return to former club Chelsea.

Lampard steered the Sky Blues to a top-flight return in August for the first time in more than 25 years after sealing the Championship title with a 5-1 win over Portsmouth, having earned the point which guaranteed promotion at Blackburn four days earlier.

However the former Blues midfielder has been linked with a third stint in charge at Stamford Bridge following the sacking of Liam Rosenior.

Lampard's stock has risen after guiding Coventry to the title in his first full season in charge and King admitted it was inevitable he would be linked in the "merry-go-round" of football.

He told BBC CWR: "He's done a fantastic job, it's been an incredible 18 months for us and for him. I am sure he's in reflective mode. I said to him 'do not underestimate how difficult what you've just achieved is to do'. He's done huge things in his playing career but to get out of this league as champions without a parachute payment, from where we've come from, is a huge achievement nobody can take away from him."

King claimed Lampard was in "a happy place" at Coventry and added: "You can see how emotionally connected he is with the city, you can see what it meant to him to get promotion and then the title and I think he's found a happy place at the moment."

King also revealed Coventry have been planning for the Premier League for a while but says simply throwing money at the challenge "would be a mistake." He said: "We've been top of the league since October. We're trying to work out a philosophy. Ultimately we will decide on what our strategy is going to be and then we will tell no one and will try and quietly, stealthily get on with it."

Asked about avoiding relegation in their first top-flight season since 2000-01, King said: "It's taken a long time to get there. I'm embracing it, the team's embracing it, it's exciting, it's a challenge. We had a challenge to get out of the Championship and we've achieved that in a spectacular way."

King said in a message to supporters: "We couldn't have done it without you. This is your success as it is mine, the head coach's and players' success."

Pakistan's Field Marshal Asim Munir has emerged as a central figure in ceasefire negotiations between the US and Iran, with President Trump publicly crediting him for requesting an extension to the two-week truce.

Hours before the ceasefire was due to expire, Trump wrote on Truth Social: "Based on the fact that the Government of Iran is seriously fractured, and upon the request of Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, of Pakistan, we have been asked to hold our attack."

Munir's global rise was rooted in a four-day war between India and Pakistan in May 2025, triggered after armed men killed 26 tourists in Indian-administered Kashmir's Pahalgam. India blamed Pakistan; Islamabad denied involvement. India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, striking targets inside Pakistan. Pakistan said it downed multiple Indian jets. A ceasefire was reached on May 10 through backchannel diplomacy involving Washington.

Trump repeatedly claimed credit for brokering the ceasefire. On May 20, Pakistan's cabinet unanimously approved Munir's promotion to field marshal, crediting his leadership during the war.

On June 18, Trump hosted Munir for lunch at the White House — the first time a US president had privately received a Pakistani military chief without civilian leadership present. Trump described Munir as "a great fighter" and "a very important guy."

Pakistan maintained channels with both the US and Iran, making it one of the few countries able to communicate with both sides during the conflict. On April 8, the US and Iran announced a Pakistan-mediated two-week ceasefire following backchannel negotiations, including direct consultations Munir held with US Vice President JD Vance, Trump's Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

In November 2025, parliament passed a constitutional amendment creating the post of Chief of Defence Forces, held by Munir, placing all military branches under unified command. The bill passed the Senate in 16 minutes. Critics argued the changes represented an unprecedented concentration of power. A retired three-star general told Al Jazeera: "External validation makes domestic consolidation more dangerous, not less, precisely because it wraps concentration of power in the language of national success."

Palestinian children in the occupied West Bank community of Umm al-Khair arrived at school to find settlers had erected a barbed wire fence blocking their path overnight, preventing them from reaching their classroom a kilometre away.

When children tried to go around the fence, Israeli soldiers launched tear gas and sound grenades at children as young as five years old. "It was a very violent situation," said Khalil Hathaleen, head of the village council. "Until now, some children haven't returned to the site because of fear. They can't sleep."

Security camera footage showed settlers erecting the fence at night without legal authorisation. Despite this, soldiers have refused to remove the barrier. The community also faces imminent Israeli demolition orders this month due to a lack of building permits — permits that are almost never granted to Palestinians in Area C of the West Bank, which is entirely under Israeli control.

Five-year-old Masa Hathaleen stood before the barbed wire and pleaded: "I am Masa. Please open the road for us. We want to go to school. We are not doing anything wrong. We just have our books. We love our school."

The path was established in 1980 and is recorded on both Israeli Civil Administration and Palestinian maps as a designated pedestrian route for students. Israeli authorities offered an alternative route roughly 3km in length, but residents rejected it because it would force children to pass through new settler outposts.

Last summer, Awdah Hathaleen was killed in that area. A settler was arrested and charged in his fatal shooting but continued returning to the village to clear land for new settler caravans. Last month, five-year-old Siwar Hathaleen was struck by a settler's car while crossing through the village. She survived but was hospitalised with a head injury.

"In any other country, if this many children couldn't reach school, the president would resign," said Khalil Hathaleen. "But here, there are no solutions apparently." Teacher Tareq Hathaleen said: "Education is a right for everyone, including the children of Umm al-Khair. It's not right to block their road."

An Israeli air strike has targeted a group of civilians in northern Gaza, killing at least five Palestinians including three children, according to Gaza's civil defence agency.

"Five Palestinians, including three children, were killed in an Israeli air strike that targeted a group of civilians near Al-Qassam mosque in Beit Lahia," local health officials said. Their bodies were taken to Al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City.

Israel has committed 2,400 violations of the ceasefire agreement with Hamas struck in October, Gaza's Government Media Office said. These included targeted strikes, arrests, blockades and forced starvation of Gaza's residents.

More than 20,000 children were killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in two years of the conflict, according to a Save the Children report. The charity said that on average at least one child was killed every hour, over 1,000 of them under one year old.

Since the US-brokered ceasefire took effect in October, at least 786 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces, according to Gaza's health ministry. At least 32 of those deaths were in April alone, among them Al Jazeera journalist Mohammed Wishah, killed in a drone strike west of Gaza City on April 8.

UN Women reported that an average of at least 47 women and girls were killed each day during the war — more than 38,000 in total between October 2023 and December 2025, including over 22,000 women and 16,000 girls. "Women and girls accounted for a proportion of deaths far higher than those observed in previous conflicts in Gaza," said Sofia Calltorp, the agency's humanitarian action head.

Israel has also been accused of violating the ceasefire by restricting agreed quantities of food, medicine and shelter materials into Gaza, where about 2.4 million Palestinians, including 1.5 million displaced, are living in desperate conditions.

With 50 days to go until the 2026 World Cup kicks off, FIFA and the tournament's host nations face criticism over wide-ranging social, political and logistical issues.

Canada and Mexico will co-host with the United States, which alongside Israel launched a war on World Cup participant nation Iran on February 28. While a fragile ceasefire is in place, Iran's participation remains uncertain. Iran had said it would not participate if the host nation could not guarantee players' security, following a social media post from President Trump suggesting that the Iranian team's safety could not be guaranteed in the US. FIFA rejected Iran's request to relocate its games to Mexico.

Fans across the three host countries are in uproar over exorbitant ticket prices. A round-trip train ride from Manhattan to MetLife Stadium costs nearly 12 times the regular fare at $150 for a roughly 15-minute ride. FIFA and New Jersey's governor have traded blame over who should cover the cost.

FIFA put tickets on sale in December at prices ranging from $140 for Category 3 in the first round to $8,680 for the final — later raised to as high as $10,990. The North American bid had initially promised tickets available for as little as $21; however, the cheapest ticket has been priced at $60.

The Trump administration's mass deportation push has also spurred concerns about whether the World Cup's international audience could be targeted by US immigration authorities. Reports suggest ICE agents were present at last year's FIFA Club World Cup matches, though the administration denied conducting enforcement.

Mexico faces separate scrutiny after a lone gunman opened fire on tourists atop the Teotihuacan pyramids, killing one Canadian tourist and injuring 13 others. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum pledged to beef up security ahead of the tournament. The tournament begins June 11 with Mexico vs South Africa.

Iran's state media and military leadership say they are prepared for a resumption of war with the United States and Israel, even as President Trump extended a ceasefire after negotiators failed to arrive in Pakistan for talks.

Authorities organised military parades on Tehran's streets timed to coincide with the ceasefire deadline. In Enghelab Square, a Khorramshahr-4 ballistic missile was moved through cheering crowds. In Vanak Square, masked men atop a truck-mounted missile launcher stood as loudspeakers blasted "Death to America."

State television has adopted a hardline approach toward negotiations. A presenter claimed, without citing a source, that 87 percent of Iranians would rather return to war than offer major concessions. The IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency released an AI-generated video showing Trump humiliated after extending the ceasefire alone.

Iran's military warned that any neighbouring country allowing its territory to be used for attacks against Iran "must say goodbye to oil production in the Middle East region." The IRGC also seized two vessels attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump said his extension decision was "based on the fact that the Government of Iran is seriously fractured" and that "Iran is collapsing financially." Iran's hardline judiciary chief responded that "the enemy is not in a position to set a time for us."

Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf offered a more moderate tone: "We are not stronger than the US in military power. It is obvious that they have more money, equipment and facilities." He framed negotiations as "a method of fighting."

President Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said: "The solution to the problems lies not in increasing tensions but in reason, dialogue and avoidance of more destruction." A Sunni religious leader warned: "The country's sky is occupied by the enemy, infrastructure is on the verge of destruction. The hardliners who today stubbornly stand in the way, what answer will they have tomorrow before God and this oppressed nation?"

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told senators that Gulf and Asian allies have requested currency swap lines from Washington to help manage the economic fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.

Bessent told a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing that the UAE and other unnamed Gulf states had formally requested the arrangements, which involve central banks exchanging currency to provide liquidity that can stabilise markets during times of uncertainty.

"Swap lines, whether from the Federal Reserve or the Treasury, are to maintain order in the dollar funding markets and to prevent the sale of US assets in a disorderly way," Bessent said. "The swap line would benefit both the UAE and the US, and numerous other countries, including some of our Asian allies, have also requested them."

Democratic senators pushed back. Senator Chris Van Hollen argued the move would put pressure on US consumers and raised concerns about the Trump family's financial ties to the UAE — including a top UAE government official's $500m investment in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, and the use of $2bn worth of its stablecoin to invest in Binance, whose founder Trump pardoned in October.

"President Trump and his family have done a very brisk business with the UAE over the last few years," Van Hollen said. Bessent denied any linkage between those ties and the proposed swap line.

About 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas passes through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively blockaded for nearly two months, causing global energy prices to soar and putting significant strain on Gulf economies. The crisis has seen the price of a barrel of oil surge above $100 at points.

Swap lines are usually approved by the Federal Reserve, but such a proposal is unlikely to pass its Board of Governors. However, the Treasury has issued currency swaps without Federal Reserve oversight before, including a $20bn arrangement with Argentina in October 2025.

The first round of the 2026 NFL Draft appears more wide open than in recent years, thanks to a lack of top-tier quarterback prospects, a concentration of premium players across non-premium positions, and relative depth at key positions.

The first overall pick is all but guaranteed to be Indiana quarterback Fernando Mendoza, selected by the Las Vegas Raiders. The bigger question is whether Alabama's Ty Simpson will join him as a first-round quarterback. Simpson is a one-year starter who impressed in the first half of the season but tailed off toward the end, reportedly while dealing with injuries. Draft analyst Connor Rogers described him as a "classic case of a day two developmental quarterback" with a ceiling similar to Denver's Bo Nix — a solid starter, but not worth a top-20 pick.

Edge rusher is one of the draft's deepest positions. Ohio State's Arvell Reese had eight sacks and 27 pressures on just 119 pass rush snaps last season, though analysts debate whether he projects better as a linebacker. Texas Tech's David Bailey posted 15 sacks and 43 hurries but weighs just 250 pounds. Miami's Rueben Bain Jr. had 12 sacks and 68 hurries but has sub-31-inch arms, which has drawn scrutiny.

Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love, Ohio State safety Caleb Downs and linebacker Sonny Styles are consistently near the top of most big boards — but teams rarely spend premium picks on those positions.

"Jeremiyah Love would be a superstar running back prospect in any draft. Caleb Downs would be as high-end of a safety prospect as you're going to see in basically any draft," Rogers said. The question is whether teams will pick the best player available or reach for a more premium position.

The biological parents of a baby at the center of an IVF embryo mix-up have been identified, according to attorneys for the Florida woman who gave birth to the infant.

Tiffany Score and Steven Mills sued the Fertility Center of Orlando after learning their newborn, Shea, was not genetically related to either of them. DNA testing revealed the baby is 100% South Asian. The clinic identified one South Asian couple from 16 sets of potential parents whose egg retrieval and embryo transfer dates matched Score's.

Score and Mills confirmed this week that a DNA match identified the baby's genetic parents, though the couple's identity would remain confidential. "This ends one chapter in our heartbreaking journey, but it raises new issues that will have to be resolved," their statement said. "Only one thing is as absolutely certain today as it was on the day our daughter was born — we will love and will be this child's parents forever."

Questions remain over what happened to the embryos believed to belong to Score and Mills, though there is no indication they resulted in a child being born to another couple. The Fertility Center of Orlando announced several weeks ago that it was closing, with another IVF network set to open in the same location.

Two doctoral students at the University of South Florida are missing, the school's police department announced. Zamil Limon and Nahida S. Bristy, both 27 and from Bangladesh, were last seen on Thursday April 16.

Limon, pursuing a doctorate in geography, environmental science and policy, was last seen at his Tampa residence. Bristy, studying chemical engineering, was last seen on the USF Tampa campus. Officials believe the two, who are friends, may be together.

Family members told NBC News the disappearance is completely out of character. Limon's brother Zubaer Ahmed said the two were "thinking about having a future together" and were dedicated to their studies. "In my wildest dream, I don't think he will do that," Ahmed said of going off the grid.

Bristy had left her laptop, iPad and lunch box behind in a university lab — only her purse and phone were missing. Limon left with his phone and wallet but his passport remained in his apartment. Bristy's family said she speaks with her parents twice a day and their last conversation on the day she disappeared was normal. Both families stressed their siblings would never willingly disappear.

The Bangladeshi Embassy confirmed that ICE told both families neither student is in its custody. Police are asking anyone with information to contact USFPD at (813) 974-2628.

Huge plumes of smoke blanketed swaths of the Southeast as crews battled rapidly growing wildfires that destroyed more than 50 homes in Georgia and forced hundreds to flee.

Some of the biggest blazes were near Georgia's coast, while others erupted in northern Florida, a state facing one of its worst fire seasons in decades. Southeastern Georgia has seen just 11 inches of rain since September — almost 15 inches below normal — prompting the state's forestry commission to issue a burn ban for the first time in its history.

Georgia's two biggest wildfires burned more than 33 square miles. The fast-moving Brantley County fire threatened roughly 1,000 homes after destroying dozens. It grew by roughly six times in just half a day. "There were fires erupting in the backyard and people taking off in the front yard," said county manager Joey Cason.

In Florida, firefighters battled more than 130 wildfires that burned 39 square miles, mostly in the northern half. "Florida has got one of the worst fire seasons in maybe the last 30 or 40 years," said state Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson. "We've been in drought for 18 months now all across the state."

Smoke drifted to Atlanta, Savannah and Jacksonville, with air quality declining to unhealthy levels in parts of south Georgia. Georgia Governor Brian Kemp declared a state of emergency for more than half the state's counties. FEMA announced approval of grants for both Georgia and Florida to battle the blazes.

The Kansas City Royals have secured $2 billion in private investment to build a new ballpark in downtown Kansas City, the team announced.

The 85-acre Crown Center project includes a park-like central square with fountains and keeps the club in Missouri. The Royals are partnering with Kansas City-based Hallmark Cards on the project, which includes the ballpark along with new headquarters for both companies and surrounding mixed-use development.

"Our founder Ewing Kauffman wanted the Royals to be Kansas City's forever," said Royals CEO John Sherman. "Joining Hallmark with this project achieves both and extends the Hall family's critical legacy of helping Kansas City grow."

The Royals have played at the 40,000-seat Kauffman Stadium since 1973. Their lease there ends in 2031. The new project will be funded primarily by the Royals and private investors, supplemented by public funding from Kansas City and Missouri's Show-Me Sports Investment Act. Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe said the announcement reinforces "that the State of Missouri is not just where the Kansas City Royals play but where they belong."

The new ballpark development will focus on walkability and access to Kansas City's streetcar network. It is expected to create more than 20,000 jobs during construction.

A suggestion by a Trump envoy that Iran should be replaced by Italy at the 2026 World Cup drew embarrassment and apathy from Italian fans and officials.

US Special Envoy Paolo Zampolli told the Financial Times he made the suggestion to both Trump and FIFA President Gianni Infantino. Zampolli, an Italian-American who is Trump's envoy for "Global Partnership" but has no official connection with the World Cup, said: "I'm an Italian native and it would be a dream to see the Azzurri at a US-hosted tournament."

The plan appears linked to an effort to repair ties between Trump and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni following a falling-out over Trump's attacks on Pope Leo XIV during the Iran war.

Italian officials were unimpressed. Sports Minister Andrea Abodi said: "Firstly it is not possible, secondly it is not appropriate. You qualify on the pitch." Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti called the idea "shameful." Coach Gianni De Biasi said: "I believe Italy doesn't need Trump's support on an issue like this. I think we can manage on our own."

FIFA pointed to Infantino's previous statement: "The Iranian team is coming, for sure. Iran has to come if they are to represent their people." Iran's football federation president said the team is "fully prepared for the World Cup." Italy missed the tournament after losing in a qualifying playoff for the third consecutive time. The World Cup begins June 11 with Iran scheduled to face New Zealand in Los Angeles on June 15.

President Donald Trump's vow to wage the biggest domestic deportation program in American history has enlisted multiple federal agencies to bolster immigration enforcement operations nationwide. Camo-clad officers are flexing their presence in cities like Los Angeles, Chicago, Memphis, Washington DC and New York, often clashing with protesters along the way.

US Customs and Border Protection has more than 60,000 employees, including about 20,000 Border Patrol agents. Two decades after its creation, the Border Patrol division has taken on an increasingly significant role in high-profile immigration actions under Trump, with agents who once apprehended migrants at borders now standing sentinel over federal immigration facilities that are sites of protests.

"These officers are not accustomed to policing urban civil unrest; nor are they trained to do so," former CBP Commissioner Gil Kerlikowske testified in a lawsuit filed by journalists over what they called "overwhelming and illegal violence" against protesters in Los Angeles. Jason Houser, a former DHS official, said agents are being put in situations they're not equipped to handle. "They're trained for border interdiction, terrorist threats, drug interdictions on swift boats. Those tactics aren't for de-escalation of a protest or riots."

In Chicago, a pastor was shot in the head with a pepper ball by agents standing on the rooftop of an ICE building — a direct violation of CBP's use of force policy. The show of force in Operation Midway Blitz even included sending speedboats to patrol the Chicago River. The CBP can legally conduct warrantless searches within 100 miles of the US border or coastline — and includes the entire Lake Michigan coastline as the "functional equivalent" of an international border. Under CBP policy, Chicago is as much of a border town as El Paso.

ICE has faced criticism for agents pulling migrants from cars, off streets and tackling people in courthouses while wearing masks. Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons defended the masks: "If it's going to keep officers safe, keep people from using advanced AI to find out their addresses and their families' information, then by all means." A federal judge in Chicago expressed concerns about agents not being clearly identified and issued an order that all agents "must have visible identification."

The Trump administration's attempt to deploy National Guard troops to major American cities under a rarely used law has faced repeated legal challenges. Both Chicago and Portland deployments were halted by federal judges who said there was no justification. The ongoing mission in DC costs about $1 million a day.

When the Trump administration secured billions in funding for the Department of Homeland Security, officials immediately kicked off an aggressive push to hire thousands more deportation officers — with up to a $50,000 signing bonus. But the effort has hit roadblocks every step of the way.

Multiple sources tell CNN that behind the scenes, ICE was ill-prepared to onboard a surge of agents in a matter of months, resulting in cut corners and people slipping through the cracks, including a DEA informant who had to be pulled out of the pool of candidates after the agency flagged them to ICE. "It's a shit show," an administration official familiar with the efforts told CNN.

White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller expressed frustration with senior ICE officials over the slow pace at which new recruits are hitting the streets, according to an administration official. By January, the agency aims to bring on board 10,000 deportation officers. The speedy hiring push has resulted in minimal background checks, absent or confusing instructions for new hires, and physically unfit people showing up to the academy.

The administration has cut down training for ICE officers to 47 days. According to sources familiar with the current process, there are no longer interviews. The agency is conducting provisional clearances with a promise of fuller background checks down the line, and officers are virtually swearing in new hires instead of doing so in person.

More than 200 people have been terminated from the academy for not meeting physical or academic standards. Former FLETC firearms instructor Robert Burnett told CNN that when he was at the academy, it was exceedingly rare for a recruit to drop out. "I would say that 97% of them would pass."

In a statement, DHS spokeswoman Tricia McLaughlin dismissed concerns and said the vast majority of new officers — more than 85% — are experienced law enforcement officers. "They're trying to do something borderline impossible and they're doing it too fast," said Scott Shuchart, former head of policy at ICE during the Biden administration. ICE alone is set to receive nearly $75 billion through 2029 under Trump's agenda bill.

The Trump administration wants Americans to have more babies, and the federal government is debuting policy initiatives to reverse the falling US fertility rate. President Donald Trump has heralded such initiatives, calling himself "the fertilization president." But reproductive rights groups say these efforts don't make up for broader administration priorities aimed at cutting federal programs that support women and children.

"Our country wants us to be birthing machines, but they're cutting what resources there already are," said Maddy Olcott, 20, a college student. "A $1,000 baby bonus? It's low-key like, what, bro? That wouldn't even cover my month's rent."

The pro-family focus, advocates say, is being weaponized to push a conservative agenda that threatens women's health, reproductive rights, and labor force participation. "The religious right wants more white Christian babies and is trying to curtail women's reproductive freedom in order to achieve that aim," said Marian Starkey of Population Connection.

Medicaid work requirements from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act will cause millions of eligible enrollees to lose coverage — and Medicaid covers more than 4 in 10 US births. The GOP also halted Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood for one year, forcing roughly 50 clinics to close since 2025. GOP spending cuts have hampered Head Start, which provides day care and preschool for young low-income children.

Just days after being sworn in, Vice President JD Vance declared, "I want more babies in the United States of America." The White House unveiled a plan for Trump Accounts — a $1,000 "baby bonus" seeded by federal funds for every eligible child born between 2025 and 2029. But data from other countries suggests such policies won't necessarily work. France, Sweden and Israel have extensive support programs, yet their fertility rates are also falling. "Nobody yet knows how to avoid depopulation," said economist Michael Geruso.

Some point to a different solution: boost immigration to ensure a younger labor force. The Trump administration is doing the opposite. The country's immigrant population fell for the first time since the 1960s this year, according to Pew Research.

The US Food and Drug Administration is reviewing evidence about the safety and efficacy of mifepristone, one of the drugs used in medication abortion, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary wrote in a letter to 22 Republican attorneys general.

Kennedy and Makary said the FDA would conduct "its own review of the evidence, including real-world outcomes and evidence, relating to the safety and efficacy" of mifepristone. "This Administration will ensure that women's health is properly protected by thoroughly investigating the circumstances under which mifepristone can be safely dispensed," they wrote.

The letter is driving concern among abortion advocates that the federal government may put new limits on access to medication abortion. Kennedy claimed in a Senate hearing that the Biden administration "twisted the data" on mifepristone to "bury one of the safety signals," but didn't provide additional details.

The Republican attorneys general cited a report from the Ethics and Public Policy Center as evidence that mifepristone is risky. But many experts consider the report to be "junk science." Dr. Ushma Upadhyay, a UCSF professor, put together a 10-point review of its major flaws. Any visit to an emergency room was counted as a serious adverse event, including visits that required no treatment. The Society of Family Planning has urged the FDA to dismiss the paper: "This paper is not a methodologically rigorous, evidence-based resource, and does not warrant consideration."

Clinical studies and decades of use have established mifepristone's safety. Since its FDA approval in 2000, there have been 5 deaths associated with it for every 1 million people who used it — a death rate of 0.0005%. Its safety is on par with common over-the-counter pain relievers. Major medical groups including the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists have repeatedly called for more mifepristone accessibility.

In 2024, there were more than 1 million abortions in the US for the second year in a row. Since the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision revoked the federal right to abortion in 2022, 20 states have enacted bans or severe restrictions.

A federal judge Tuesday refused to block filling prescriptions for the abortion pill mifepristone by mail across the US — at least for now — in a setback to Louisiana's effort to stifle groups that send it into states where abortion is banned.

US District Judge David Joseph, nominated by President Donald Trump, ruled against Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill, who asked that FDA rules allowing mifepristone to be dispensed through the mail be paused while a challenge to those 2023 regulations moves through the courts. He granted the government's request to put the case on hold, though warned the pause would not be indefinite.

"Should the agency fail to complete its review and make any necessary revisions to the rules within a reasonable time frame, the Court's analysis will inevitably change," he wrote. He also said he believes the plaintiffs are "likely to succeed on the merits."

Murrill said she would ask an appeals court to throw out the federal rules, noting the judge "concluded that Louisiana suffers irreparable harm every day" the current rules are in effect. Murrill contends that allowing mail prescriptions undermines Louisiana's abortion ban, one of 13 states that bar abortion at all stages of pregnancy.

"From the courts to the Trump administration to state legislatures across the country, mifepristone and abortion access are very much still under attack," Planned Parenthood Federation President Alexis McGill Johnson said.

One study found that by the end of 2024, one-fourth of abortions were accessed by telehealth — a fivefold increase in two years. Another study found that in 2025, women in states where abortion is banned were more likely to obtain one by getting pills through telehealth than by traveling to other states. Eight states now have laws protecting providers who prescribe abortion pills by telehealth and mail them into states with bans.

Murrill is pursuing criminal cases against two doctors accused of sending pills to patients in Louisiana. Those states have not been willing to extradite the doctors. A Louisiana woman who joined the lawsuit says her boyfriend coerced her into taking mifepristone. Arguments surrounding coercion became a major theme for the plaintiffs, who say without in-person requirements, intimate partner abuse will only increase.

The Trump administration has cut more than 4,000 employees from some of the nation's top law-enforcement agencies, even as it vowed to crack down on crime, according to records obtained by Reuters under the Freedom of Information Act.

The total number of employees at the FBI has dropped more than 7% since the government's 2024 fiscal year, a loss of about 2,600 people. The Drug Enforcement Administration's staff dropped by about 6%, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives lost about 14% of its workers. The Justice Department's National Security Division, which handles intelligence and terrorism matters, lost nearly 38% of its staff.

"It's the difference between being proactive and entrepreneurial or purely reactive to the most obvious imperative of the day," said Adam Hickey, a former senior official in the National Security Division.

The contraction, combined with an increased focus on immigration, has caused authorities to pull back from typical work. Last year, federal prosecutions for drug trafficking dropped to their lowest level in more than two decades, and the government is bringing even fewer such cases this year.

Justice Department spokeswoman Natalie Baldassarre said, without offering evidence, that buyouts allowed the agency to shed people who "did not want to aggressively and faithfully tackle crime." She said that with the US murder rate at its lowest in recent history, "any suggestion that this reduction in force has hampered our ability to tackle violent crime is not based in reality."

The department's Civil Rights Division lost more than half its staff. The Bureau of Prisons — which its own internal watchdog has said is in a "staffing crisis" — shed more than 2,200 employees. As a result, some guard posts have gone empty and others have been staffed with teachers and nurses pulled from their regular positions.

"The administration talks a big game when it comes to crime and terrorism, but the fact that it's hollowing out agencies tasked with addressing them shows that they don't stand behind their words," said Stacey Young, a former Justice Department lawyer.
